outcomes.text: Understand information given as text, tables and diagrams.
Pull out the information relevant to the problem.
Combine data taken from related data sets.
Understand descriptions of simple models, such as calculation instructions with thresholds or rules to follow.
Identify necessary and sufficient conditions.
Work out facts about original data from a summary of processed data.
Use one or more items of information to solve a problem, working out the needed operation.
Apply a model, such as a calculation or a simulation over time, to a situation.
Search all possible solutions for those meeting given criteria, and count them if asked.
Find which criteria a proposed solution fails to meet.
Draw conclusions from information and the relationships between items.
Compare the consequences of different options to choose the best.
Infer reasons for patterns in numerical data.
Recognise equivalent representations of the same data, such as pie chart and bar chart.
Spot features of an object that identify it after rotation or other transformations.
Read features of a model from different representations, such as a graph's gradient.
Suggest explanations for trends, including changes in trend at a point.
Find model parameter values so the model fits available data, such as a price per kilometre.
Consider how a change to a scenario, such as a road closure, may require adjusting a solution.
Identify features of a situation the model should include when it does not fit the information.
Adjust a model to include extra features and judge the options against the information.
Judge reliability of a source: reputation, ability to observe, vested interest, expertise and bias.
Judge plausibility of a claim regardless of its source.
Tell corroboration from consistency and inconsistency between pieces of evidence.
Judge whether a sample is large enough.
Judge how the method of selection may bias a sample.
Judge whether a sample represents the group the claim is about.
Spot misleading presentation of data, such as truncated axes, uneven intervals or symbol sizes.
Assess an explanation for evidence, noting if it leaves evidence unexplained, relies on speculation or has equal rivals.
Assess an inference from evidence, including factors that weaken support.
Suggest an explanation for evidence.
Suggest an inference from evidence.
Form a judgement from several sources.
Tell an argument apart from explanation, information and opinion.
Identify key elements: main conclusion, intermediate conclusion, reason, counter-assertion, counter-argument, example and evidence, and what each does.
Identify unstated assumptions needed for the conclusion to follow.
Recognise equivocation and conflation, and how they weaken reasoning.
Recognise circular argument and begging the question.
Recognise invalid deduction (affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent).
Recognise causal flaws (post hoc and cum hoc).
Recognise rash and sweeping generalisation.
Recognise restriction of options (false dichotomy).
Recognise confusion of necessary and sufficient conditions.
Recognise the slippery slope argument.
Recognise personal attack (ad hominem) and counter-attack (tu quoque).
Recognise the straw man argument.
Judge weaknesses of support: reasoning that backs only part of a conclusion or needs a stronger claim.
Judge weaknesses of consistency: parts that contradict each other.
Judge weaknesses of reliance: dependence on a questionable unsupported claim, definition or assumption.
Judge appeals (authority, popularity, emotion, tradition, novelty) as relevant or irrelevant.
Judge analogies, and failure to respond to an obvious counter.
Articulate a conclusion and give reasons for it.
Develop strands of reasoning and structure them with intermediate conclusions.
Strengthen reasoning with counter-argument and response, examples, evidence, analogy and hypothetical reasoning.
